children.text: Use evidence to correct museum labels about fossils, soils and light.
Print the shared evidence, one response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the worked answers. Prepare an oral, pointing or adult-scribed route where useful.
Use this as an honest synthesis and evidence review, not a claim that these topics are all new. Optional clean sealed samples may support observation.
No digging, tasting, crumbling fossils or handling unknown soil is required. Use printed evidence or clean sealed samples.
If using a lamp, use a cool low-power LED and keep it away from eyes. Never view the Sun.
All core reasoning uses the supplied evidence and can be completed in 40 minutes without a live practical.
Supported: Short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed reasons; same core scientific goal.
Standard: Make a short evidence-based explanation or record using the supplied information.
Stretch: Apply the core idea to a changed case, evaluate evidence or identify a limit.
Regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer seated observation, quiet paired rehearsal, private feedback and a pass from public sharing. Routes respond to current access needs, not a diagnosis.
1 ancient life: remains or traces. 2 relevant soil component. 3 receive light.
W1 A is the ancient fossil; B is a recent model, based on their stated histories. W2 soil is a mixture, including mineral and organic material; eyes receive light from the lamp-lit exhibit.
Second option correct. The first ignores when B was made; the third contradicts C’s organic material.

S1 A. S2 any two recorded components: mineral grains, decayed leaf matter, air or water. S3 into the eye. S4 e.g. this fossil preserves evidence of an ancient shell; soil contains a mixture; reflected light reaches the eye.

M1 A has geological preservation; B was made today. M2 e.g. soil contains mineral grains and organic matter, with pore spaces. M3 lamp → fossil surface → eye; arrows into eye. M4 exact original colour is unknown from this record.

T1 some rocks contain fossils, but a stone need not preserve remains or traces of life. T2 no: the record explicitly says unknown. T3 E states that the same fossil remains but no light reaches the eye. T4 a fresh leaf is recent organic matter; ordinary falling into soil is not evidence of ancient preservation.
E1 ancient remains or traces of life. E2 e.g. organic matter, water, air or a living organism. E3 light, here reflected from the exhibit.
Responses vary. Credit a scientific revision, evidence-based defence or relevant next question. A private or oral response has equal value.

Adult pilots a low ramp so the block slides without tumbling or snagging and stops within the tray. Fix the ramp and transition; use the same block/contact face and marked release point without a push.

The supplied constructed distances allow the full lesson without equipment. For real trials measure from the ramp end to the same trailing block edge at stopping; use three releases per surface and keep actual results separate.
Keep the activity on a stable table in a contained tray with a stop barrier. No pupils sliding on floors or ramps.
Use a small block, low ramp and clear release area; keep hands out of its path. No heavy falling objects or stretched elastic launchers.

W1 rubber, 14–16 cm compared with card 58–62 cm and cloth 22–24 cm; it fits shorter run-out here. W2 an extra push changes starting conditions; repeat from the same release mark without a push and annotate the flawed run.
First option correct. Friction on the right-sliding block points left; contact force persists after release.
S1 rubber. S2 14,15 or16 cm. S3 left. S4 same block/contact face, ramp/release point, transition, distance rule or other relevant condition. S5 no: changes start conditions.

M1 change horizontal surface; measure run-out distance in cm. M2 card 58–62 cm; rubber 14–16 cm, rubber shorter in every run. M3 friction opposes relative sliding, acts left on right-moving block and slows it after release. M4 fix ramp and mark; same block/face; release without push; measure from ramp end to same trailing edge at rest; repeat three runs per surface and retain records.

T1 rubber gave the shortest run-out for this wooden block/contact face and controlled setup. T2 friction depends on the pair, surface condition and loading; a different use needs relevant evidence. T3 card, about 60 cm here. T4 record the bunching/snag and affected run, secure the strip flat with comparable transition, repeat under the stated method and distinguish snagging from normal sliding resistance.
E1 relative sliding between block and surface. E2 rubber. E3 fixed ramp angle/release mark, same block face, no push or comparable transition.
Responses vary. Credit a scientific revision, evidence-based defence or relevant next question. A private or oral response has equal value.

attrs.data-teacher: Think aloud: “I begin with water in soil, enter a root and follow xylem through the stem to a leaf. Some water evaporates and leaves as vapour.” Evaporation from leaves helps pull water upward; a straw-sucking mouth is not the mechanism.

children.text: Selected water path in a rooted plant: soil water enters roots, travels upward in xylem through the stem, reaches leaves, and some leaves as water vapour. Arrows do not imply that all absorbed water is lost or that root uptake was demonstrated by a cut shoot.
These water-carrying pathways are called xylem.

T1 torn paper is a valid counterexample; a physical change can be hard to reverse. Look for formation of new substances. T2 gases escaped and oxygen entered from the air as a reactant. GROW SCIENCE · The plant reproduction strategy studio
Cases are constructed teaching examples using the stated biological processes.
Pollen from one pea plant reaches another. A male and female gamete fuse before the seed develops.
A flower receives its own plant’s pollen. Male and female gametes fuse before a seed develops.
A horizontal stem grows from a parent. It roots at a node and forms a daughter plant without gamete fusion.
A piece of a parent stem roots and grows into a new plant. No gamete fusion occurs in this route.
A fictional nursery wants to preserve a parent mint plant’s inherited features. It can use cuttings; growth conditions still need care.
Clones usually share inherited information, apart from changes such as mutations. Conditions affect appearance. Some plants can make seeds without fertilisation; identify the stated process.
W1. Sort A–D into sexual/asexual and cite the deciding phrase.
W2. Recommend a route for the mint nursery and one condition to control.

A wind; B external animal attachment; C animal ingestion. Rotor exceeds compact in all trial pairs: 1.4/0.8, 1.5/0.9, 1.3/0.7 seconds. Adding a clip changes mass as well as shape; match mass. W3 bounded paper fall-time conclusion, not all real seed distances.
A correct. B no distance measured. C intention is not the measured variable.
Air; animal fur; 1.4, 0.8, rotor; any stated control; no, paper indoor descent time is not an outdoor distance measurement.

Wing interacts with air/slows descent; hook attaches to fur; animals can ingest fruit and later pass surviving seeds. N2 correct paired values/units. N3 shape changes; mass, release height/rule and airflow controlled; time to floor measured. N4 added mass is another changed factor. N5 rotor took longer in this setup; limits include paper structure, indoor still air and no distance measurement.

T1 compact (0.8+0.9+0.7)/3=0.8 s; rotor (1.4+1.5+1.3)/3=1.4 s; difference 0.6 s. T2 longer descent may allow more wind influence, but actual distance depends on many conditions. T3 vary one shape under fixed airflow setting, release height and model mass; repeat and measure horizontal landing distance in cm. It is a planning task, not an instruction to improvise a fan practical now. T4 useful inherited structures can aid dispersal; individuals do not develop them because they want a ride. Evolutionary detail is optional.

Correct structure–mechanism link; accurate pair and seconds; not real outdoor distance; relevant control/purpose. Secure: mechanism, fair variable distinction, numerical result and limit. Re-teach overclaim by underlining seconds and asking what was actually measured. Reflection accepts a precise next variable or measurement.

A = 60 × 70 = 4,200 mL/min = 4.2 L/min. B = 90 × 60 = 5,400 mL/min = 5.4 L/min. Difference = 1.2 L/min. B is greater. Heart rate alone ignores stroke volume.

Area-only pair X/Z: concentration difference 4 and thickness 1 are unchanged. X = 12, Y = 12, Z = 24. X/Y changes area and thickness together, so it cannot isolate one factor. Index units are relative, not calibrated physiological units.

Raised glucose stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin. Insulin signals responsive tissues and promotes uptake and glycogen storage in liver/muscle; blood glucose moves towards its usual range. Glucose is a transported material; glycogen is its storage carbohydrate. Some uptake is insulin-independent.

Ventilation replenishes alveolar air; oxygen diffuses into pulmonary blood, is carried by circulation to tissue capillaries and diffuses towards cells, where it supports aerobic respiration. Pump output alone omits oxygen content, distribution, exchange performance and tissue demand. Any two explained limitations are valid.
C = 120 × 35 = 4,200 mL/min = 4.2 L/min, equal to A and below B. C has the highest heart rate but not the highest output. Both factors matter.
Keep concentration difference 4 and thickness 1; use area 9. Predicted index = 9 × 4 / 1 = 36, three times X. Other assumptions and the proportionality constant must also match.

At the same output, less oxygen per unit blood could reduce oxygen delivery. Greater tissue oxygen demand could make the same delivery insufficient. These are conditional mechanisms; the supplied data do not measure either quantity or identify a person’s condition.

Example: B has greater volume output than A, 5.4 versus 4.2 L/min. This does not establish adequate oxygen supply to every tissue. Measure oxygen content of the supplied blood and specify tissue demand to test that stronger claim. Accept another coherent conclusion/limit/measurement trio.

R1: blood; R2: respiration and material use/storage; R3: the original departure. W1: A→B→C→D. W2: glucose units, not insulin, are stored as glycogen; insulin signals the processes. W3: no exact concentrations, times or individual parameters are supplied.
Correct: raised glucose stimulates more insulin release and uptake/storage responses. Insulin is not converted into glucose. The model supplies no dosing information.

After absorption raises blood glucose, pancreatic beta cells release more insulin into blood. Insulin-responsive tissues alter glucose handling; some body cells increase uptake and liver/muscle glycogen storage is promoted.
Insulin=chemical messenger hormone; glucose=sugar/material; glycogen=store of joined glucose units. A hormone signal changes cell processes; it is not the bulk material being stored.
Uptake by insulin-responsive tissues such as muscle and storage as glycogen in liver/muscle help remove glucose from blood, tending to reduce the raised concentration.
As glucose moves towards the suitable range, the stimulus for extra insulin release reduces. The response counteracts the original rise rather than amplifying it indefinitely.

No. The model has no calibrated concentrations, real time scale, individual physiology, absorption details or measured response parameters. Similar qualitative patterns need not have identical numerical values or timing.

Some tissues take up glucose through insulin-independent routes. Better: insulin promotes uptake/storage responses in particular tissues, including increased uptake in muscle cells; it does not control every uptake route in every cell.

Lower glucose stimulates pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon. Glucagon promotes liver glucose release, including glycogen breakdown, tending to raise blood glucose towards usual levels. Insulin responds to raised glucose and promotes uptake/storage; both reduce their original departure. Core success does not require glucagon.

A time/concentration axis with defined units could support comparing measurements. The relationships and parameters would still need testing against independent measured data; adding an axis alone does not show the model predicts accurately for different individuals.

Pulmonary artery carries blood away from heart, so it is an artery. Pulmonary veins carry relatively oxygen-rich blood towards heart. Muscle supplies pumping pressure; valves direct flow.
Use the full route above. Septum separates left and right sides, limiting mixing of the two streams in the normal adult heart.
An artery is defined by blood travelling away from the heart, not its oxygen content. The pulmonary artery runs from right ventricle towards lungs.
P: 80 × 55 = 4400 mL/min = 4.4 L/min. Q: 100 × 70 = 7000 mL/min = 7.0 L/min. Difference 2600 mL/min= 2.6 L/min.

Pressure differences open/close valve leaflets, preventing backflow. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to produce the higher pressure for systemic circulation. In stable circulation average outputs of the two sides match.
Need stroke volume too. R: 120 × 35 = 4200 mL/min; S: 70 × 70 = 4900 mL/min. S has lower heart rate but greater output because its stroke volume is much larger.
Some moved blood returns backwards rather than progressing through the circuit; useful net forward flow can be lower than gross chamber movement.
Because the circuits connect, persistently unequal average outputs would cause blood to accumulate in one part and deplete another. The thicker wall is primarily a pressure adaptation.
Output is a volume per time, so 5400 mL/min (if those were the measured volume data), not beats/min. Heart rate uses beats/min; a unit alone cannot diagnose health.

E1 right ventricle. E2 higher systemic pressure. E3 60×90=5400 mL/min = 5.4 L/min. Secure core: route direction, pressure/valve mechanism and valid output units. Re-teach using away/towards if pulmonary vessels are misclassified.

R1 photosynthesis. R2 soil moisture is non-living/abiotic. R3 one sample is incomplete and may miss organisms or species.

W1 e.g. soil moisture affects plant growth, or light affects photosynthesis; aphid feeding is biotic. W2 fewer aphids may reduce food for ladybirds and lead to fewer ladybirds, but alternative prey, movement or other factors can affect the outcome. W3 both have 20 individuals; A records 2 species and B 4. B has greater recorded richness in these samples. These data do not prove a cause or full-site biodiversity.
A wrong: equal abundance does not mean equal richness. B correct and limited to the evidence. C wrong: sampling variation and confounding factors are unresolved.

S1 soil moisture. S2 non-living. S3 correct arrow sequence; leaves are eaten by aphids, aphids by ladybirds, transferring material and energy. S4 two/four/twenty. S5 samples vary and one small area may miss species; more comparable samples improve the estimate.

N1 abiotic: light→photosynthesis or soil moisture→plant growth; biotic: feeding or a justified competition example. N2 e.g. leaves → aphids → ladybirds and leaves → caterpillars → blue tits. Fewer aphids may reduce ladybird food; other prey/movement/interactions create uncertainty. N3 abundance 20 both; richness A 2 / B 4. N4 repeat equal-area samples at randomly selected locations in both patches using comparable identification and effort; one unmatched observational comparison does not isolate maintenance from other factors.

T1 the count measures recorded plant richness in small samples, not all biodiversity in the whole garden; causal attribution to mowing is unsupported. Accurate rewrite: “Our equal-area sample from B recorded four plant species, compared with two in A; further sampling is needed.” T2 sample several randomly selected equal-area quadrats in each defined patch, at comparable times with the same counting/identification rules and equal effort; record relevant conditions. To test mowing causally, use replicated comparable plots with assigned regimes and before/after measurements where feasible. T3 aphid feeding damage may fall; ladybirds may lose prey; blue tits could lose aphids as prey but have other food. The web omits many foods, movements, abundance and timings, so exact size or certainty cannot be inferred.

E1 abiotic environment and interactions with living organisms. E2 ladybird consumes aphid; transfer from food to consumer. E3 individuals can be distributed among different numbers of species. E4 repeated randomly located equal-area samples reduce selection bias and show variation; common method/equal effort improve comparability. Reflection accepts a relevant evidence-seeking question and reason.

Secure core: explains an ecosystem interaction, reads food-to-consumer arrows, and gives A 2 / B 4 richness while recognising abundance 20 each and a sampling limit. Re-teach reversed arrows with “is eaten by”; re-teach richness confusion by counting only rows with non-zero values before adding individual counts. Formal diversity indices, trophic efficiency and population equations are not required.

R1: down a concentration gradient; R2: oxygen; R3: respiration differs from breathing. W1: P/Q changes area only; Q has twice the index. W2: P/R changes thickness only; R has half the index. W3: less fresh-air replacement can reduce alveolar oxygen and the oxygen gradient as exchange continues.

Ventilation moves air because volume/pressure changes. Oxygen diffuses into blood across alveoli. Cellular respiration releases energy in cells. Correct hinge: thin barrier shortens diffusion distance; diaphragm does not directly force oxygen across membranes.

Oxygen arrow air→blood; carbon dioxide arrow blood→air under the stated gradients. Ventilation replenishes air and removes carbon dioxide; blood flow brings relatively oxygen-poor blood and carries exchanged gases away, helping maintain differences.

During inhalation diaphragm contracts/flattens and external intercostals raise ribs up/out; thoracic volume rises, pressure falls below atmospheric and air enters. Quiet exhalation involves relaxation and elastic recoil, reducing volume and raising pressure so air leaves.

P/Q differs only in area: Q faster. P/R differs only in thickness: R slower. Inputs are relative and idealised, so no clinical concentration, saturation or measured exchange rate can be read from the index.

Large total area supports more simultaneous exchange; a thin alveolar/capillary barrier shortens the diffusion path; moisture enables gases to dissolve. Gradients and blood/air replacement are also important. Cellular respiration is an energy-releasing process in cells, not air movement.
P = 2 × 4 / 1 = 8; Q = 4 × 4 / 1 = 16; R = 2 × 4 / 2 = 4. Q/P = 2; R/P = 0.5. The numerator uses concentration difference; these are relative indices with the same proportionality constant.
Unchanged: twice the area divided by twice the thickness gives the original index if the concentration difference and other model assumptions match.
Small cube 6:1; larger cube 24:8=3:1. The larger cube has less surface per unit volume; increasing size can make diffusion-only exchange less adequate for its volume, depending on shape and demand.
Idealised uniform barrier/gradient, no real units or diffusion coefficient, no changing blood flow/ventilation, no heterogeneous alveoli or individual physiology. Any two specific limits are valid.

E1: pressure falls as volume increases, so air moves in from higher external pressure. E2: shorter diffusion distance. E3: accurate ventilation/diffusion versus respiration distinction. Secure core requires a mechanism, not a feature list; reteach with one gas arrow and one pressure arrow.

R1 blood. R2 ventilation moves air; diffusion is net particle movement down a concentration gradient. W1 M = 3,000 mL/min = 3 L/min; N = 4,000 mL/min = 4 L/min. W2 target-cell recognition/responsiveness matters. W3 pulmonary artery is an artery because it leaves the heart. Output alone does not establish health. Correct hinge: record support, attempt first and review afterwards.
Q1: 4 marks, same across all routes

Award one mark each: pancreas [1]; insulin [1]; one valid response such as increased glucose uptake in responsive tissues or increased glycogen storage in liver/muscle [1]; blood glucose decreases towards its usual range [1]. Do not require beta-cell terminology. Do not credit insulin becoming glycogen. Some glucose uptake is insulin-independent.
Q2: 4 marks, same across all routes

Lungs → left atrium [1] → left ventricle [1] → aorta [1] → body. Artery carries blood away from the heart [1]. Accept LA/LV if meaning is clear. Oxygen-rich is not a sufficient definition; pulmonary artery is the counterexample.
Q3: 4 marks, same across all routes

A: 75 × 80 [1] = 6,000 mL/min [1]; 6 L/min [1]; output also depends on stroke volume, so heart rate alone is insufficient [1]. Accept consistent error-carried-forward for the conversion method if a previous arithmetic slip occurred. If B is used as evidence: 100 × 50 = 5,000 mL/min = 5 L/min, despite its higher heart rate. A correct unsupported final 6 L/min can receive the result and conversion marks, but not the explicit-working mark.
Q4: 4 marks, same across all routes

Thoracic volume increases [1]; pressure falls below atmospheric/surrounding air pressure [1]; oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into arriving blood down its concentration gradient [1]; a thin barrier shortens diffusion distance [1]. For the third mark require direction and gradient. Cellular respiration and ventilation alone do not name the exchange mechanism.
Q5: 4 marks, same across all routes

Thickness changes, from 1 to 2 [1]. V = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6 [1]. U = 12, so V has half U’s index [1]. One specific limit [1]: relative uncalibrated inputs, omitted proportionality/diffusion coefficient, uniform fixed barrier/concentration difference, no changing blood flow or ventilation, or no tissue-demand information. Do not accept only “it is a model” without explaining the limitation. Allow consistent comparison reasoning after an arithmetic slip; do not award two marks for one unexplained value.

A defensible answer identifies oxygen content, distribution to the relevant tissue, exchange effectiveness and/or tissue oxygen demand as additional evidence. Explain why a volume per minute alone cannot show oxygen adequacy. Do not use this answer to add marks to the 20-mark core.
